clues: Represents the majority of adverse drug reactions in clinical practice.
Predictable from known pharmacology and dose-dependent.
An exaggerated or augmented extension of a drug's normal pharmacological action.
Unrelated to a drug's normal dose-response pharmacology.
Includes idiosyncratic drug responses and immune-mediated allergies.
An unpredictable, bizarre adverse drug reaction often requiring drug withdrawal.
An X-linked enzymopathy affecting the pentose phosphate pathway in red blood cells.
Reduces NADPH needed to maintain reduced glutathione during oxidative stress.
Predisposes patients to acute haemolysis after taking primaquine, dapsone, or sulfonamides.
Triggered by succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics such as halothane.
Involves uncontrolled calcium release from skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum.
A hypermetabolic anesthetic emergency with rigidity and high fever treated with dantrolene.
Develops after prolonged blockade of dopamine D2 receptors by antipsychotics.
Features involuntary movements of the tongue, lips, and jaw.
A late-onset hyperkinetic movement disorder often persistent after antipsychotic exposure.
Triggered by dopamine receptor antagonists such as haloperidol.
Marked by lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and high creatine kinase.
A rare, life-threatening drug reaction to antipsychotics treated with drug stop, dantrolene, or bromocriptine.
Can occur when SSRIs are combined with MAO inhibitors or linezolid.
Causes agitation, autonomic hyperactivity, hyperreflexia, and clonus.
A toxic state of excess serotonergic activity in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Involves extensive epidermal detachment over more than 30% of body surface area.
Often affects mucous membranes and carries a positive Nikolsky sign.
A severe, life-threatening exfoliative drug reaction related to Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and St John's wort are classic triggers.
Increases synthesis of metabolizing enzymes such as cytochrome P450.
Accelerates metabolism of co-administered drugs, lowering their plasma levels and efficacy.
Develops over repeated doses of opioids, nitrates, or benzodiazepines.
Means the original dose produces a smaller response than it did initially.
Reduced responsiveness to a drug after repeated administration requiring a higher dose for the same effect.
Seen between morphine and heroin or between ethanol and benzodiazepines.
Occurs among agents acting on shared receptors or pathways.
Tolerance to one drug that reduces the effectiveness of another related drug.
Results from neuroadaptation to chronic drug exposure.
Precipitated abruptly by giving naloxone to an opioid-dependent patient.
A physiological state in which stopping a drug or giving an antagonist triggers a withdrawal syndrome.
Includes lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, and cramps in opioid cessation.
Can cause seizures and delirium tremens when severe after stopping alcohol or benzodiazepines.
Characteristic physical and psychological symptoms emerging when a dependent drug is stopped.
A positively charged protein that binds negatively charged anticoagulant molecules.
Reverses bleeding caused by unfractionated heparin.
The specific antidote used to neutralize heparin.
An oxime given alongside atropine in organophosphate poisoning.
Must be given before the inhibited enzyme undergoes irreversible aging.
Reactivates acetylcholinesterase inhibited by organophosphate insecticides.
Can precipitate withdrawal or seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients.
Acts competitively at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors.
The specific antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine sedation.
Helps convert oxidized ferric iron in haemoglobin back to the ferrous oxygen-carrying state.
Relies on NADPH and should be used with caution in G6PD deficiency.
The reducing antidote used to treat drug-induced methaemoglobinaemia.
Also known as folinic acid.
Used as rescue therapy after high-dose methotrexate.
A reduced folate that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase inhibition to rescue normal cells.
Involves antibodies against complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4.
Causes low platelets paradoxically accompanied by venous or arterial clots.
An immune-mediated complication of heparin therapy requiring stopping heparin and starting an alternative anticoagulant.
